title: Optional and Named Arguments

content.intro: Optional and Named Arguments is lesson 47 in Methods and Reusable Code. A method names a unit of behavior, with explicit inputs and an explicit result or side effect. Keep its responsibility narrow and test meaningful edge cases.
content.why_it_matters: Small methods give a program testable units and make intent visible. This lesson focuses on optional and named arguments and shows how to verify the behavior instead of relying on assumptions.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: A method names a unit of behavior, with explicit inputs and an explicit result or side effect. Keep its responsibility narrow and test meaningful edge cases.

content_blocks.title: A practical way to learn it
content_blocks.text: Start with the smallest valid case for optional and named arguments. Predict the output, run or inspect the example in the stated toolchain, then change one input or rule and compare the result. For production code, record assumptions and verify boundary cases.

items.title: Optional parameters
items.text: Design methods around one responsibility, clear inputs, and a clear result. Prefer ordinary value parameters by default; use overloads and modifiers only when they make the contract easier to understand.

items.title: Default argument values
items.text: Pick a parameter-passing form that communicates ownership and intent; avoid ref/out when a returned value is clearer.

items.title: Named arguments
items.text: Design methods around one responsibility, clear inputs, and a clear result. Prefer ordinary value parameters by default; use overloads and modifiers only when they make the contract easier to understand.

items.title: Argument ordering rules
items.text: Pick a parameter-passing form that communicates ownership and intent; avoid ref/out when a returned value is clearer.

items.title: Public API design considerations
items.text: Use explicit timeouts, parameterized database commands, small service boundaries, and validation for external results.

content.task: Try it yourself: create a small C# example that demonstrates optional and named arguments. Change one input or implementation detail, predict the result, then check it locally and explain one edge case.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates optional and named arguments rather than only repeating its definition.
The result is checked locally or against a clearly documented reference output.
At least one relevant boundary, invalid-input case, or compatibility condition is considered.
hints: List the assumptions and expected behavior for optional and named arguments before editing the code.
Change one variable or rule at a time; keep the previous output for comparison.
If behavior differs, confirm the compiler/target framework and consult the linked official documentation.
content.solution_notes: Suggested approach: identify the expected input and output, start from the smallest example, use the feature only where it clarifies the rule, and verify both a typical case and a boundary/failure case.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming the feature works identically on every target
common_mistakes.why: Language syntax, libraries, and runtime support are version-dependent.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the target framework and official versioned reference before using the feature.

common_mistakes.why: Boundary values, malformed input, and failure states often expose the real bug.
common_mistakes.fix: Add one typical input and one boundary or invalid case to the manual or automated checks.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating sample output as proof that the code ran
common_mistakes.why: The course reader uses static reference output for C# because it has no C# execution runner.
common_mistakes.fix: Run the snippet in a local .NET project or a separately isolated execution service.
